```{r setup}
library(idmapper)
library(dplyr)
```

## The problem

Say you help run a community running club, and you want to join together
three datasets that all describe the same runners, but were extracted from
different systems that don't share a common key:

- **`race_results`** - from the race-timing company that ran last month's
  10k. One row per runner, identified by whatever **email** they used when
  registering for the race.
- **`fitness_app_leaderboard`** - from a GPS running app some members use to
  track their training. One row per runner, identified by their **app
  username**, and whatever **email** they signed up to the app with - which
  is sometimes the same email they registered for the race with, and
  sometimes a different one entirely.
- **`club_roster`** - the club's own membership system. One row per member,
  listing their **member ID**, **app username**, **race-registration
  email**, and **app-signup email** all together.

None of this data is real - it's entirely synthetic, invented for this
example.

```{r}
race_results <- tribble(
  ~runner_name,      ~race_email,                       ~finish_time_minutes,
  "Jordan Blake",    "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",   47.2,
  "Sam Okafor",      "sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com",     52.8,
  "Nora Fitzgerald", "nora.fitz@fictionalmail.com",      61.5,
  "Yusuf Demir",     "y.demir@fictionalmail.com",        44.9
)

fitness_app_leaderboard <- tribble(
  ~app_username, ~app_email,                        ~total_distance_km,
  "jblake_runs", "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",   412,
  "samo_runs",   "samokafor.trains@fastmail.com",    298, # different email to race_results!
  "yusufd",      "y.demir@fictionalmail.com",        520
)

club_roster <- tribble(
  ~member_id, ~app_username,  ~race_email,                      ~app_email,
  "M001",     "jblake_runs",  "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com", "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",
  "M002",     "samo_runs",    "sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com",   "samokafor.trains@fastmail.com",
  "M003",     NA,             "nora.fitz@fictionalmail.com",    NA,
  "M004",     "yusufd",       "y.demir@fictionalmail.com",      "y.demir@fictionalmail.com"
)
```

Notice **Sam Okafor**: `race_results` has the email he registered for the
race with, but `fitness_app_leaderboard` has a different email entirely -
the one he happened to sign up to the running app with years earlier.
Those two rows share *no* identifier directly - the only place that
connects them is `club_roster`, which happens to list both of his emails
side by side.

A plain join on email will simply miss him:

```{r}
naive_join <- race_results %>%
  left_join(fitness_app_leaderboard, by = c("race_email" = "app_email"))

naive_join %>% select(runner_name, race_email, total_distance_km)
```

Sam's `total_distance_km` comes back `NA` - not because he doesn't use the
app (he's logged 298 km on it), but because the join has no way to know
`sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com` and `samokafor.trains@fastmail.com` are the
same person. You could patch this one case by hand, but that doesn't
scale, and you won't always have a human around to notice the mismatch.

## Solving it with idmapper

The idea: instead of joining datasets directly to each other, treat every
identifier (an email, a username, a member ID) as a node, and link two
nodes whenever they co-occur on the same row of the same dataset. Two
datasets that never share an identifier directly can still end up in the
same connected component if a third dataset bridges them - exactly Sam's
case.

### 1. Initialise an identity graph

```{r}
init_id_envs("person")
```

### 2. Mark identifier columns, and add each dataset to the graph

`mark_id()` tags a column with the entity type (`"person"`) and the kind of
identifier it holds. `add_to_identity_graph()` reads those tags and updates
the graph. A dataset can mark - and link - more than one identifier type at
once, which is exactly what makes `club_roster` useful here: it contributes
both of Sam's emails *and* his app username and member ID, all linked to
each other because they're on the same row.

```{r}
race_results <- race_results %>%
  mark_id(race_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%
  add_to_identity_graph()

fitness_app_leaderboard <- fitness_app_leaderboard %>%
  mark_id(app_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%
  mark_id(app_username, graph = "person", type = "username") %>%
  add_to_identity_graph()

club_roster <- club_roster %>%
  mark_id(race_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%
  mark_id(app_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%
  mark_id(member_id, graph = "person", type = "member_id") %>%
  mark_id(app_username, graph = "person", type = "username") %>%
  add_to_identity_graph()
```

### 3. Collapse the graph into master identities

```{r}
master_runners <- generate_master_identity_table("person")
master_runners
```

Four runners in, four master identities out - as expected, since every
person here is a genuine distinct individual. (If two *different* people
had accidentally shared an identifier - a mistyped email reused by two
membership records, say - this is the step where you'd see them wrongly
merged into one row, which is why it's worth eyeballing this table rather
than trusting it blindly on a new data source.)

### 4. Attach master IDs back onto each dataset, and join on those instead

```{r}
race_results2 <- race_results %>% join_master_ids()
leaderboard2  <- fitness_app_leaderboard %>% join_master_ids()

race_results2 %>% select(runner_name, person_UID)
leaderboard2 %>% select(app_username, person_UID)
```

Now join on `person_UID` instead of on email:

```{r}
combined <- race_results2 %>%
  left_join(
    leaderboard2 %>% select(person_UID, total_distance_km),
    by = "person_UID"
  )

combined %>% select(runner_name, finish_time_minutes, total_distance_km)
```

Sam Okafor's `total_distance_km` now correctly shows `298` - resolved via
the club roster bridge, with no special-casing required. Nora Fitzgerald
correctly shows `NA`: she's a genuine race finisher who's never used the
training app, not a matching failure - the identity graph didn't invent a
leaderboard record for her, it just didn't find one.

## Restricting a new dataset to known people

Suppose a fourth dataset arrives - say, RSVPs for a club social run - and
you only want to keep rows for people already known to the identity graph
(as opposed to, say, guests who are tagging along but aren't club members).
`filter_by_existing_identities()` does this without adding any new
identifiers or edges to the graph:

```{r}
social_run_rsvps <- tribble(
  ~attendee_name, ~attendee_email,
  "Jordan Blake", "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",
  "Sam Okafor",   "samokafor.trains@fastmail.com", # his app email - still resolves, it's in club_roster
  "Talia Reyes",  "talia.r@example.com"            # a friend tagging along, not a club member
)

social_run_rsvps %>%
  mark_id(attendee_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%
  filter_by_existing_identities(env_name = "person")
```

Talia Reyes is dropped: her email never appeared anywhere in the graph.
Sam Okafor is kept even though the RSVP list has his *app* email rather
than the one he registered the race with - because `club_roster` already
linked that app email to the rest of his identity.

## Summary

- Mark identifier columns with [mark_id()], add each dataset to the graph
  with [add_to_identity_graph()].
- [generate_master_identity_table()] once, after every dataset has been
  added.
- [join_master_ids()] to attach a resolved ID to any dataset, then join
  datasets to each other on that ID instead of on a raw identifier.
- [filter_by_existing_identities()] to restrict a new dataset to only
  people/entities already known to the graph.

The payoff over a plain `left_join()` is specifically in cases like Sam's:
two records that share no identifier directly, but are transitively linked
through a third dataset. The more data sources you have, the more of these
bridges tend to exist - and the more a naive pairwise join quietly misses.
